## Goal

By the end of this exercise you should have:

- **built a Shiny app** with the agent that lets someone filter, plot and summarise a dataset,
- **run it on your own computer** and **checked its numbers** against a spreadsheet,
- **tried to break it** (nothing selected, no matching rows, missing values) and made it fail politely,
- **exported it with Shinylive** and previewed the static version, after reading exactly which files it contains, and
- **published an app for your own project** next to your page, with a written decision about what data may be public.

Your session will look different from anyone else's, and so will your app. Compare **the numbers it shows**, not its looks.

## Before you start

- You have R installed (*Terminal survival kit*, *Reproducible figures*). If your figures script from *Reproducible figures* is in Python, you can do the whole exercise with Shiny for Python instead; the notes below say where it differs.
- You have a page for your project in its own page folder, published on GitHub Pages from `docs/` (*A course or project page*). You need it only for the last part.
- Make the folder `~/agentic-course/shiny-apps/water-app` (Windows: `C:\Users\<you>\agentic-course\shiny-apps\water-app`) and download the example data into it:

| Download | What it is |
|---|---|
| [water-quality.csv](data/water-quality.csv) | 288 invented water samples from four invented sites, 2022–2024: `site`, `date`, `temperature_c`, `ph`, `nitrate_mg_l`, `oxygen_mg_l`. Six values are missing on purpose. |

- Open the CSV once in Excel or LibreOffice and look at it for a minute. (If the numbers look wrong, for example 72 instead of 7.18, it is your spreadsheet's regional setting: import it with **Data → From Text/CSV**, comma as separator and point as decimal.)

::: {.callout-note}
**Privacy.** The example data is synthetic and may be published. Your own data in the last part may not be. Read the privacy step there **before** you give the agent your data.
:::

## Worked example

### Step 1: Ask for the app

Start the agent in the `water-app` folder:

::: {.panel-tabset}
## Claude Code
```bash
cd ~/agentic-course/shiny-apps/water-app
claude
```
Manual mode is fine: you approve each file and command.

## Codex
```bash
cd ~/agentic-course/shiny-apps/water-app
codex
```
The folder is not a git repository, so Codex may start read-only. Type `/permissions` and choose the mode that lets Codex edit files in this folder (not full access).
:::

Type this prompt:

```text
water-quality.csv has water samples from four sites (one row per sample:
site, date, temperature_c, ph, nitrate_mg_l, oxygen_mg_l). Some values are NA.

Make a Shiny app in app.R so that colleagues can answer questions like
"how did nitrate at Mill Creek change in 2023?" without asking me.

Inputs: tick boxes for the sites (all ticked at start), a date range, a menu
for the measurement (with readable names and units), an option for a trend line.
Outputs: a plot of the measurement over time, one colour per site; a table
per site with the number of samples, the number missing, mean, min and max;
the first 20 selected rows; a button to download the selected rows as CSV.

If no site is ticked or no rows match, say so in plain words. Count missing
values; never drop them silently. Use only shiny and ggplot2.
Tell me how to start the app, and one number I can check by hand.
```

For **Shiny for Python**, replace `app.R` with `app.py` and the last packages sentence with "Use only shiny, pandas and matplotlib."

**What to look for.** The agent writes one file, `app.R`. If the R package `shiny` is not installed, it asks to install it: read the command and approve. If it wants other packages, ask why, and whether it can do without. At the end it should tell you how to start the app.

### Step 2: Run the app on your computer

The simplest way is to ask:

```text
Start the app and tell me the address to open in my browser.
```

Open the address (it starts with `http://127.0.0.1:`). If the agent cannot keep the app running while you use it, ask it for the exact command and run that yourself in a **second** terminal window, in the same folder:

| | R | Python |
|---|---|---|
| Start | `Rscript -e "shiny::runApp()"` | `shiny run app.py` |
| Stop | Ctrl+C in that terminal | Ctrl+C in that terminal |

If you use RStudio, you can instead open `app.R` and press **Run App**.

`127.0.0.1` means "this computer": nobody else can open the app. After every change to `app.R`, stop the app and start it again (or reload the browser, if the app restarts by itself).

### Check the result

1. **One number by hand.** In the app, tick only **Mill Creek**, set the dates to **2023-01-01** to **2023-12-31**, and choose **nitrate**. Write down the number of samples and the mean. Then, in the spreadsheet, turn on the filter (Data → Filter), filter `site` to Mill Creek and `date` to 2023, and select the `nitrate_mg_l` cells: the status bar shows the count and the average. Both must say **24 samples, mean 2.66**.
2. **A second number.** Do the same for **Alder Lake**, 2023, nitrate: **24 samples, mean 0.60**. An app that is right for one setting can be wrong for another.
3. **Missing values.** Choose **oxygen**, **North Pond**, 2023. The table should say **24 samples, 4 missing, mean 11.78**. If it says 20 samples and nothing missing, the app drops missing values silently. If it says `NA`, it does not handle them. Both need fixing.
4. **Break it.** Untick every site. Then tick one again and set the dates from **2022-01-06** to **2022-01-18** (between two sampling days). In both cases the app should show a short message in plain words, not a red error and not an empty plot without explanation.
5. **The download.** Choose a setting, press the download button, and open the file. Does it have the same number of rows as the app reports?
6. **The edges of the dates.** Set the dates from **2024-12-19** to **2024-12-19**, the last sampling day. The app should show 4 rows (one per site). If it shows 0, the date filter leaves out the end date.

If a check fails, say exactly what you saw and what you expected:

```text
For oxygen at North Pond in 2023 the table says 20 samples and 0 missing.
The data has 24 samples there, 4 of them NA. Count the NA values in the
"missing" column and compute the mean from the rest.
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Expected outcome"}
- One file `app.R` of roughly 60–150 lines, using `shiny` and `ggplot2`.
- Mill Creek, 2023, nitrate: 24 samples, 0 missing, mean 2.66, min 1.49, max 3.65.
- Alder Lake, 2023, nitrate: 24 samples, 0 missing, mean 0.60, min 0.32, max 0.89.
- North Pond, 2023, oxygen: 24 samples, 4 missing, mean 11.78.
- All four sites, all dates: 288 rows. Missing values in the whole file: 4 oxygen (North Pond, June–July 2023) and 2 pH (Stone River).
- A reference version of the app is [example-app/app.R](example-app/app.R). Yours does not have to look like it, but it must give the same numbers.
:::

### Step 3: Export it with Shinylive and preview it

Now turn the app into a static site that runs in the browser. Stop the running app first (Ctrl+C). Start the agent in the **parent** folder `~/agentic-course/shiny-apps`, so that the export can go next to the app, and type:

```text
Export the Shiny app in water-app/ as a static Shinylive site into the
folder water-app-site/. Install the shinylive package if needed (ask me
first). Then list every file from water-app/ that ended up in the export,
start a local preview server, and tell me the address.
```

**What to look for.** For R, the agent uses the R package `shinylive` (`shinylive::export(...)`) and previews with `httpuv::runStaticServer(...)`. For Python, it uses the Python package `shinylive` (`shinylive export ...`) and `python3 -m http.server`. The first export downloads the Shinylive files once, which can take a minute.

Check:

1. **The file list.** It should contain only `app.R` and `water-quality.csv`. Everything on that list is published if you publish the export.
2. **It runs in the browser.** Open the preview address. The first load is slow (R is downloading into the browser). Then the app should look like the one you ran before.
3. **Same numbers.** Repeat check 1 (Mill Creek, 2023, nitrate: 24 samples, mean 2.66) in the static version.
4. **It needs a server.** Close the preview, then double-click `water-app-site/index.html` in your file browser. You get a blank page or an error. That is expected: unlike the demo in *Interactive demos*, a Shinylive export must be served by a web server, such as the preview command or GitHub Pages.
5. **The data is in the browser.** In the preview, open the browser's developer tools (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac), go to the **Network** tab and reload. Look through the files the page downloads, for example `app.json`. Can you find the rows of `water-quality.csv`? Every visitor can do the same.

::: {.callout-tip}
If the export fails because a package is not available in the browser, ask the agent to replace it with one that is, or to remove the feature. Keeping to `shiny` and `ggplot2` (or `shiny`, `pandas` and `matplotlib` in Python) avoids most problems.
:::

## On your own project

Now build an app for data from your own project and publish it next to your page, **if** the data may be published. If it may not, you build the app for local use, and publish a version with aggregated or synthetic data, or nothing at all.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Privacy reminder.** A Shinylive app publishes its whole data file to every visitor. Personal data, sensitive data, data given in confidence and unpublished data that is not yours to release must **never** go into a Shinylive app. Also remember that the agent reads the data while it builds the app, which sends it to the provider: follow the precautions in your README for your data class.
:::

### Step 1: Decide what may be public

Open your project's README and look at the data class you wrote in *Privacy, ethics and safety*. Then decide, using the table from the lecture:

| Your data | What you do |
|---|---|
| Public or synthetic | build the app on it and publish with Shinylive |
| Internal (no people), owner agrees to publish | as above; write down who agreed and when |
| Internal, owner does not agree, or you have not asked | app for local use only; publish nothing, or ask about a university server |
| Personal or sensitive | no public app; build the app on a synthetic or aggregated stand-in, and check that no small groups remain |

Ask the agent to record the decision:

```text
Add a section "Data app" to README.md with: the questions the app should
answer, the data file it uses, the data class, whether the app may be
published (and who decided), and how I will check its numbers. Use my
answers below and do not invent anything.

My answers: <write your answers here>
```

If you need a stand-in, ask for one: "Make a synthetic dataset with the same columns, ranges and number of rows as `<file>`, and a script that generates it. Do not copy any real values." Then check that it really contains no real rows.

### Step 2: Build and check the app

Start the agent in your **project folder** and ask for the app in a subfolder, for example `apps/<name>/`, containing **only** `app.R` (or `app.py`) and the data file it needs. The app's source stays in the project; only its export will go to the public page folder. Adapt the prompt from the worked example: start from the questions in your README, list the inputs and outputs, and keep the sentences about empty selections and missing values.

Then do the same checks as in the worked example:

1. **Two numbers by hand** in a spreadsheet, for two different filter settings.
2. **Missing values** are counted, not dropped.
3. **Break it:** nothing selected, no matching rows, the first and last date.
4. **The download** has as many rows as the app says.

Write the two hand-checked numbers into the README section. Commit.

### Step 3: Publish it next to your page

Only if Step 1 said the data may be public. Exit the agent, go to your **page folder** and start the agent there:

```text
Export the Shiny app in ../<my-project>/apps/<name>/ with Shinylive into
the folder <name>-site/ in this website. Add a page explorer.qmd,
"Data explorer", that says in two sentences what the data is, where it
comes from and its licence, that the first load takes a few seconds,
and links to <name>-site/ (or embeds it with an iframe). Add the page
to the sidebar. List <name>-site under resources in _quarto.yml, next
to .nojekyll, so that rendering copies it into docs/. Render the site.
Then list every data file that is now in docs/, with its size.
```

1. **Read the list of data files.** Is every file on it one you are allowed to publish? If not, stop and fix it before you commit.
2. Preview the site (ask the agent to start a local preview server for `docs/`; double-clicking does not work for the app), open the app and repeat one hand-checked number.
3. Commit (including `docs/`) and push. Wait a minute or two for GitHub Pages.
4. Open the **published** page on your laptop and on your phone. Wait for the first load. Repeat one hand-checked number on the published version.
5. Add a line to the **Log of AI use** section of your README: what the agent built, which checks you did, and the publishing decision.

If the data may **not** be public, skip the export. Keep the app in your project for local use, and write in the README how to start it. If you think a university server would help, ask your IT department whether one exists, and add their answer to the README.

## What you should have now

- `~/agentic-course/shiny-apps/water-app/app.R`: a checked app for the example data, and `water-app-site/`, its Shinylive export, previewed locally.
- In your project folder: `apps/<name>/` with an app for your own data (or a stand-in), and a README section with its questions, data class, publishing decision and two hand-checked numbers.
- If your data may be public: the export in your page folder and a "Data explorer" page on your published site, checked on a laptop and a phone.
- A new line in the Log of AI use.
